results.name: single_example_yes_gap
results.description: Yes-rate on single-example sets minus yes-rate on multi-example sets (non-example targets only); observed above null means the model under-generalizes from one example (too narrow), below means it over-generalizes.
results.code:
# name: single_example_yes_gap
# description: Yes-rate on single-example sets minus yes-rate on multi-example sets (non-example targets only); observed above null means the model under-generalizes from one example (too narrow), below means it over-generalizes.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    inset = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    a = (n == 1) & (~inset)
    b = (n > 1) & (~inset)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: early_session_yes_gap
results.description: Yes-rate in the first 90 trials of a session (trial_index < 90) minus yes-rate in later trials; the model has no time dependence, so observed below null means people start more conservative and become more liberal over the session (and vice versa).

results.name: first_example_digit_lift
results.description: Among multi-example sets without a shared final digit, yes-rate on non-example targets sharing the FIRST example's final digit (but not the last's) minus yes-rate on targets sharing no example's final digit; the model gives only the last example a lingering digit, so observed above null means a primacy digit effect the model misses.
results.code:
# name: first_example_digit_lift
# description: Among multi-example sets without a shared final digit, yes-rate on non-example targets sharing the FIRST example's final digit (but not the last's) minus yes-rate on targets sharing no example's final digit; the model gives only the last example a lingering digit, so observed above null means a primacy digit effect the model misses.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    inset = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    D = np.mod(E, 10)
    dmin = np.nanmin(D, axis=1); dmax = np.nanmax(D, axis=1)
    ok = (n >= 2) & (dmin != dmax) & (~inset)
    td = t % 10
    first = D[:, 0]
    last = D[np.arange(len(t)), n - 1]
    anyd = np.any(D == td[:, None], axis=1)
    a = ok & (td == first) & (td != last)
    b = ok & (~anyd)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: pair_yes_rate_dispersion
results.description: Standard deviation across (set, target) pairs of the pair-level yes-rate; observed above null means human judgments are more all-or-none (more extreme, more set/target-specific) than the model's graded overlap probabilities, below means the model is too extreme.

results.name: same_decade_yes_gap
results.description: Yes-rate on non-example targets sharing a tens digit (same decade) with some example minus yes-rate on non-example targets sharing no decade; observed below null means people avoid same-decade targets more than the model predicts, above means decade similarity the model lacks.
results.code:
# name: same_decade_yes_gap
# description: Yes-rate on non-example targets sharing a tens digit (same decade) with some example minus yes-rate on non-example targets sharing no decade; observed below null means people avoid same-decade targets more than the model predicts, above means decade similarity the model lacks.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    inset = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    sd = np.any(np.floor(E / 10) == np.floor(t / 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    a = sd & (~inset)
    b = (~sd) & (~inset)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: parity_violation_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on targets of the opposite parity to a multi-example set whose examples all share one parity but not one final digit; observed above null means people honour the shared parity less than the model predicts (model over-weights parity), below means parity is a harder constraint than modelled.
results.code:
# name: parity_violation_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate on targets of the opposite parity to a multi-example set whose examples all share one parity but not one final digit; observed above null means people honour the shared parity less than the model predicts (model over-weights parity), below means parity is a harder constraint than modelled.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    inset = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    P = np.mod(E, 2)
    allodd = np.nansum(P == 1, axis=1) == n
    alleven = np.nansum(P == 0, axis=1) == n
    D = np.mod(E, 10)
    dmin = np.nanmin(D, axis=1); dmax = np.nanmax(D, axis=1)
    samedig = dmin == dmax
    m = (n >= 2) & (~samedig) & ((allodd & (t % 2 == 0)) | (alleven & (t % 2 == 1)))
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[m].mean())

results.name: near_miss_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on targets 1-3 away from the nearest example (target not itself an example) minus yes-rate on all other non-example targets; observed below null means people reject near neighbours more than the model (which has no proximity term) predicts, above means numeric similarity generalization the model misses.
results.code:
# name: near_miss_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate on targets 1-3 away from the nearest example (target not itself an example) minus yes-rate on all other non-example targets; observed below null means people reject near neighbours more than the model (which has no proximity term) predicts, above means numeric similarity generalization the model misses.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    inset = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    near = (dist >= 1) & (dist <= 3)
    other = (~near) & (~inset)
    if near.sum() == 0 or other.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near].mean() - r[other].mean())

results.name: large_target_yes_gap
results.description: Yes-rate on non-example targets outside the examples' range [min,max] that lie above the max minus those below the min (multi-example sets); observed above null means people extend generalization upward more readily than downward beyond what the model's fitted bound saliences predict.
results.code:
# name: large_target_yes_gap
# description: Yes-rate on non-example targets outside the examples' range [min,max] that lie above the max minus those below the min (multi-example sets); observed above null means people extend generalization upward more readily than downward beyond what the model's fitted bound saliences predict.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    inset = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    ok = (n >= 2) & (~inset)
    a = ok & (t > hi)
    b = ok & (t < lo)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
